articles.text: Monday, August 11 signaled the start of another school year in Piedmont. Piedmont kids, teachers and parents have pronounced summer vacation finished, and school in session. A dreary sky hung over the first morning of school before the first bells rang at 8:30 a.m. Many kids and parents beamed as kids wore their best and brightest outfits with new haircuts and new backpacks. One big change this year for all Piedmont elementary students will be the switch to Fishtank Learning for the English Language Arts curriculum. This year’s elementary music curriculum is being called a bridge year according to the school district, to be used to perfect a more permanent change coming in 2026- 27 . This year, Piedmont fourth graders will take Theater Arts instead of music and 5th graders will essentially double up on their music instruction time. At Beach Elementary, Principal Anne Valva has quickly become the most tenured principal in the district. Valva and PMS’s Karen Shipp both became principals in 2022. Valva has quickly found a home leading her school, with the support and respect of her staff and students. On the three elementary school campuses, parents said goodbye and took photos beneath purple and white balloon arches, holding signs with friends. “And what’s your name?” a Beach teacher asked one of her new students. “I don’t think I’m ready for this,” a Beach mom said while holding the hand of a three-year old. At Wildwood, new Principal Amy Fry got off to a fast start. “The first day was great,” she said. “I enjoyed seeing so many students and families excited to return to school. I’m looking forward to working with the community to help continue to make Wildwood a wonderful place to learn and grow.” Havens students now only need to remember one important name: Reed. New Principal Susanne Reed and office Administrative Assistant Melanie Reed share the name and look to form an administrative synergy as well. Tender goodbyes and enthusiastic I-love-yous were seen on the playgrounds of all three schools. At Beach, those farewells visibly had more immediacy and lingered on longer, towards the lower side of the playground, where the youngest students’ Kinder and T-K journeys begin. Hugs and kisses from moms and dads started the day off. At 8:30 a.m. students filled into their new classrooms, with new knowledge to be imparted, friends to be made and memories to form. The first day of school by and large is a reunion for students in Piedmont between friends formerly long lost, but now reunited.

By Pastor Jim Hopkins Dear Lala: You are four and one half years old now and on Monday you are going to start T-K (Transitional Kindergarten). You have gone to your new school many times before but now it is not only their school; it is your school. YaYa and I simply want to say that we hope you will have the time of your life and that we think it is very likely that you will. You know that Hop Pop works at a church. Sometimes you come and sit on the steps with me when I talk to the kids and tell them stories. Sometimes you go with the other kids and Miss Yvonne while the big people stay in church. Sometimes you stay with your mom and dad and listen to the people sing and to Hop Pop talk. Sometimes when I’m doing that, we give each other a little wave. The Big Book I read from tells us that God creates each and every one of us, that God knows us and that we are “fearfully and wonderfully made.” I don’t expect you to understand those words, I don’t understand them completely myself, but I hope you will remember that their message is that you are magnificent, precious and irreplaceable. You will not always go to Hop Pop’s Church but if you ever go to another church that, for whatever reason, tells you that you are not magnificent, precious and irreplaceable, please get out of that church as fast as you can. The world we live in can be very hard. That is one of the lessons we learn when we watch Bluey together. Sad things happen. We make mistakes and messes. So do other people. Still, hard and sad things are not all there is. There is family, there is laughter, there is imagining and there is love. I don’t know what your favorites things to learn about and do will be. Take a good long time to figure that out. Try lots of things. Don’t worry if it isn’t easy. Remember the Bluey episode “Baby Race” where everybody was worried about who did what first? It didn’t really matter, did it? What mattered was trying, learning and accepting that everyone was different. Another thing the Big Book that Hop Pop reads from says is that God doesn’t give everyone the same talent but that everyone is given a gift. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is surveying residents on potential programs to help transition homes from natural gas to clean electricity. Feedback will guide which pilot programs, like bulk purchasing or smart panels, should be prioritized. Residential natural gas use accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions. Piedmont’s Sustainability Division is working with a community task force to understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a practical, equitable framework for solutions – a potentially vital part of achieving the city’s climate goals. The online survey builds on earlier community input that identified the biggest barriers to home electrification in Piedmont. Now, the task force is exploring possible programs the city could pursue to help address those barriers. Feedback on these concepts will help determine which ideas to prioritize for further analysis. The survey asks for input on four program concepts: • Organizing neighborhood electrification projects to lower costs through bulk purchasing. • Providing short-term appliance loans while property owners make upgrades needed to support electric equipment. • Launching a pilot program to test “smart panel” devices that help residents electrify their homes without expensive panel upgrades. 2025 Sustainability James Glauber talks about his induction cooktop, which heats pans directly and efficiently. Residents can check out the City’s Induction Cooktop Lending Program to try out this cooking technology for free. For each program, the survey asks: • How well could this help address common barriers to home electrification? • Which program would be most helpful for you personally? • If the city could only do one of these programs, which would you prioritize? The survey should take about five minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ElectrificationSurvey. Piedmont’s climate goals Natural gas use in residential buildings accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, homes are on average less energy efficient than those in neighboring communities. Transitioning these buildings from natural gas to renewably sourced electricity not only has health, safety, and cost benefits, it is a critical part of meeting the City Council’s adopted goal of climate neutrality by 2045. The city has convened an Electrification Task Force of community representatives— covering a broad range of expertise and experiences—who are working with sustainability staff to develop a roadmap for supporting all community members in switching to electric appliances. For more information on the Electrification Strategy and Electrification Task Force, including meeting materials, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ElectrificationStrategy. With questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun at dergun@piedmont.ca.gov. 2025 Sustainability Awards Winner James Glauber shows his home battery and heat pump. articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. My husband David and I, and our neighbors, are very concerned about the safety ramifications of the Moraga Canyon housing plan, mainly: 1. Evacuation route: Moraga Ave. is a principal evacuation route for Piedmont and Oakland. We can’t imagine 900 additional daily trips on top of the existing 11,000. Last night at the Planning Commission meeting, your outside consultant said that the bike lane would be used as an emergency third lane. Very dangerous for any pedestrians/bikers escaping in an emergency. Not safe! 2. We worry about potential fire insurance increases/insurability denials for both Oakland and Piedmont neighbors as a result of packing in 197 units in a fire zone. 3. How will you provide parking for 197 units on the Blair side of Moraga? Your diagram shows 130 units. 4. An alternate site would be to consolidate 3 elementary schools into 2. Enrollment decreases every year; you actively recruit Oakland students, causing Oakland to lose state funding. Your headcount per school site is very low compared to cities of comparable size. articles.text: The Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD) has issued a work notice about upcoming environmental investigation activities at the former Shell service station at 29 Wildwood Avenue in Piedmont. Work will include soil, vapor, and groundwater testing as part of cleanup oversigh. Beginning Aug. 14, Wayne Perry, Inc. and Shell will conduct environmental surveys over three days. The work will be carried out in accordance with permits from the Alameda County Public Works Agency and overseen by ACEHD. Work will take place from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday through Friday, and will include the use of a limited-access direct push rig and support vehicles. The site, which Shell plans to redevelop into an electric vehicle charging station, is currently regulated by ACEHD under a Leaking Underground Storage Tank case and a Cleanup Program Site case. To confirm that current site conditions in the soil, soil vapor, and groundwater are protective of utility workers and nearby properties, crews will install five soil vapor probes six inches beneath the building foundation and five more probes four feet deep inside and outside the existing building. Once this work is complete, the site will be secured until ACEHD approves the removal of the building foundation and hydraulic hoists. A separate work notice will be issued before demolition and lift removal. Based on investigation results, ACEHD may require cleanup actions. Residents will be notified of any further environmental work through fact sheets and public meetings. Community protection measures The work notice outlines the following protective steps during the investigation: • Plastic sheeting will protect the work area and prevent soil transfer to asphalt. • Inspect and/or clean vehicle wheels before leaving the site. • Maintain straw bales to stop dirt, silt, or slurry from entering storm drains • Maintain fencing and posted signage with a phone number for complaints. According to the notice, dust and odors will be controlled. Residents with concerns may call Tracy Craig at 510-334-4866 for a prompt response. The notice also invites residents to review the case file for the 29 Wildwood Avenue project, including all technical documents, online at the State Water Resources Control Board GeoTracer website at https://geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov and searching for the address “29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont.” map of the site boundary and sample locations at 29 Wildwood Ave.

articles.text: 1-year-old, 57-pound Sway is turning heads and winning hearts. This Husky mix is a mix of young-dog energy and older-dog obedient. Environmental investigation at former Shell Station to begin Aug. 14 By Tony Simons The Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD) has issued a work notice about upcoming environmental investigation activities at the former Shell service station at 29 Wildwood Avenue in Piedmont. Work will include soil, vapor, and groundwater testing as part of cleanup oversigh. Beginning Aug. 14, Wayne Perry, Inc. and Shell will conduct environmental surveys over three days. The work will be carried out in accordance with permits from the Alameda County Public Works Agency and overseen by ACEHD. Work will take place from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday through Friday, and will include the use of a limited-access direct push rig and support vehicles. The site, which Shell plans to redevelop into an electric vehicle charging station, is currently regulated by ACEHD under a Leaking Underground Storage Tank case and a Cleanup Program Site case. To confirm that current site conditions in the soil, soil vapor, and groundwater are protective of utility workers and nearby properties, crews will install five soil vapor probes six inches beneath the building foundation and five more probes four feet deep inside and outside the existing building. Once this work is complete, the site will be secured until ACEHD approves the removal of the building foundation and hydraulic hoists. A separate work notice will be issued before demolition and lift removal. Based on investigation results, ACEHD may require cleanup actions. Residents will be notified of any further environmental work through fact sheets and public meetings. Community protection measures The work notice outlines the following protective steps during the investigation: • Plastic sheeting will protect the work area and prevent soil transfer to asphalt. • Inspect and/or clean vehicle wheels before leaving the site. • Maintain straw bales to stop dirt, silt, or slurry from entering storm drains • Maintain fencing and posted signage with a phone number for complaints. According to the notice, dust and odors will be controlled. Residents with concerns may call Tracy Craig at 510-334-4866 for a prompt response. articles.text: Students returned to the Piedmont Middle School campus last week with walkthrough registration in the Buzz Redford Gym. On Friday, August 8, students had their photos taken for school ID cards wearing brand new shirts, picked up schedules and happily ran into classmates from days gone by. PMS Principal Karen Shipp stood in the doorway of the gym taking it all in. Shipp said there wasn’t much new about walkthrough registration this year, but that there is always such excitement and energy every year as students reunite with their friends. New 6th-8th graders received their class assignments and compared schedules with friends not seen since before summer vacation. Inside the gym students also got Scots Camp t-shirts, and visited a variety of tables for signups for extracurricular activities. articles.text: Football season opens August 30 Piedmont High’s football team is back on the field with helmets cracking and pads smacking as they build toward their August 30 season opener at Salesian. The Highlanders opened padded practice on Monday, August 11, officially turning the page on last year’s 10-2 result and the WACC Mission Division title. Piedmont won their second straight league title in 2024 after winning the 2023 Shoreline Division crown. They reached the Division 7 NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed before losing to No. 2 Ferndale, but a 42-46 NCS win over No. 6 Fortuna marked the school’s first postseason win since 2017. “I’ve been waiting for this day since last November,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We want to get that taste out of our mouth. We have a really different team; it’s going to require a lot of teaching this year.” Last year’s team concluded a cycle that saw 16 seniors graduate. Offensive and defensive lineman Adrian Kondakov is set to start at left tackle and is the only returning starter from last year’s offensive front. “It’s difficult having four new people to teach but it’s fun being with a new group,” Seiden said. “I’m trying to teach them to have a gritty mentality and to push themselves when they are tired. As long as guys come every day to practice with the mentality of getting better, they’ll become a good varsity player.” Kondakov is expected to lead by example. Seiden describes him as a man of few words. Staff Photos Adrian Kondakov is the only returning starting offensive lineman from last year and will start at left tackle. “The only senior in that group is Adrian. He’s a silent leader. He’s one of my four-year kids and I’ve maybe heard him say 10 words. He nods his head and goes to work. He’s very intelligent and loves football after never playing before coming to high school,” Seiden said. Of the 16 graduates from 2025, Piedmont faces the task of replacing three-year starting quarterback Markos Lagios. As it turns out, the school will continue having a Lagios in the No. 4 slot at quarterback. The position will be filled by Markos’ younger brother, Jimmy Lagios, who. is taller than his older brother and slings the ball with as much spin and velocity. Jimmy was the Post’s honorable mention for 2025 Freshman of the Year. “The irony of him being Markos’ brother isn’t lost on me. But he’s just scratching the surface. He played really well on JV, so we Jimmy Lagios is stepping into the starting quarterback role, wearing the same number as his older brother Markos, who as the quarterback last year. Xavier Henderson enters his senior year as a key playmaker on offense, defense, and special teams. just want to see his progression. As that’s happening. He’s going to be a huge part of whatever we’re able to do,” Seiden said. With a vast number of starters to replace on both offense and defense, Piedmont’s running game could become a strong point. Xavier Henderson looks like the Highlanders’ feature back, while Colby Hong provides downhill power and Rehan Mumtaz adds speed to the mix. Henderson came to the school last year and made an instant impact. He’s now one of the leaders om the team. “I look at it with a positive outlook. My mentality is really no different from last year, it’s just about showing up and wanting it more – the type of player who goes all out and becomes a different person on the field. I’m looking to carry that on this year,” Henderson said. Henderson was a playmaker for Piedmont in all three phases. He had 169 rushing yards and one touchdown, to go with 19 pass receptions for 312 yards and six touchdowns last year. He also led the team in tackles for loss, and had two kickoff returns for touchdown. Yet he is entering the 2025 season feeling like he has something to prove. “I have a lot to prove this year. I really want to get a scholarship offer and to just improve overall. I’m just trying to bond with the guys and get better,” Henderson said. The Highlanders’ full football program is looking set to have around 55 athletes spread across varsity and junior varsity, the highest number in years. The varsity program will have around 30 athletes, a far cry from where the program was in 2022 when the varsity was canceled midway through the season. Now, Piedmont can run 11-on-11 practices with both units. “It almost makes you choke up seeing where the program is now, especially the original coaches who have been here the whole time when we had 15 kids,” Seiden said. After back-to-back WACC titles, Piedmont isn’t looking to lay off the gas. If all goes well, the Highlanders could be competing for their second straight Mission Division title. articles.text: Staff Photos I traveled to Bangkok to watch Tottenham Hotspur play a preseason match, but torrential downpour canceled the match. All I got was this crummy picture of Harry Kane, who now plays for Bayern Munich. If you’ve been following the Post’s sports section over the last couple of years, you may remember my recount of a trip to Thailand to watch my favorite European football team, Tottenham Hotspur of North London, for their preseason tour. The trip in 2023 to Bangkok’s Rajamangala Stadium was spoiled by a monsoon, making the pitch sopping wet and unplayable. Parents, coaches, and students at Piedmont High have come to notice me wearing a Tottenham hat or jersey of Heung-min Son and Lucas Moura It’s often been a topic of conversation between and the English-born coaches at Witter Field over the years, like boys’ soccer coach Todd Russell who support Southampton, former boys’ coach Todd Sullivan who is a devout Manchester United supporter, and former girls’ coach Dan Chubbock. In 2022, I traveled to Ibrox Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland to watch Tottenham take on Rangers. It gave me a chance to watch manager Antonio Conte’s new team and see my favorite players, Son and Harry Kane, in person for the first time. As professional sports go, 2022 marked Kane’s final year at the club, finishing his time as Tottenham’s greatest player of all time and its all-time leading goal scorer. Moura was cut loose in May 2023. My focus for my 2023’s preseason trip to Rajamangala Stadium was to say goodbye to the greatest striker the club has ever produced before the English captain was traded to German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season in late July. Rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a waterlogged pitch that caused balls to stick like arrows into the grass. With just six crew members A photo of the monsoon rain pouring down at Rajamangala Stadium. It remains one of my fondest travel memories. A photo of Heung-Min Son in 2022 at Ibrox Stadium. He now plays for LAFC of Major League Soccer. working to clean the full 100-plus yard field, locals turned to me and laughed, saying: “Welcome to Thailand.” As the rain poured while we huddled underneath an overhang of Rajamangala Stadium, little did I recognize how vast the changes at Tottenham would occur since I last saw them in person in July 2023. In addition to Kane and Moura leaving before the 2023-24 season, Conte was fired near the end of 2023 after going on a rather comical tirade during a press conference. Tottenham hired Ange Postecoglou as their next manager, known for his attacking brand. Nearly two years later, Postecoglou and Son helped lead Tottenham to the Europa League title in May following a season of frustration. Tottenham finished the Premier League season in 17th of 20 teams, just one spot above the relegation zone, after injuries hobbled the lineup from start to finish. Regardless, Spurs made it to the Europa League Final in Bilbao against Manchester United, winning 1-0 to give Tottenham its first trophy in 17 years. But change was immediately on the horizon. In the weeks after lifting the Europa League trophy, Postecoglou was fired due to their 17th place finish in the Premier League. Since that day in Rajamangala, Spurs have held onto just 13 players out of 40 going into 2025-2026, including both of my favorite players, Son and Kane, now elsewhere. Unfortunately, the Post’s vacation schedule the last two years haven’t lined up with Tottenham’s preseason tour. This year, the club played in Hong Kong against Arsenal and in Seoul versus Newcastle. But more importantly, Son announced he was departing from Tottenham Hotspur following their August 3 match against Newcastle, ending his time with the club after 10 years of service. He now plays for LAFC in Major League Soccer, at least giving me more chances to watch him in person in the U.S., albeit for a different team. The changes throughout Tottenham since my last trip to watch them are an unmistakable reminder of the vicious cycle of professional sports. All I got was this crummy picture of Harry Kane, who now plays for Bayern Munich. By Jonathan Comeaux If you’ve been following the Post’s sports section over the last couple of years, you may remember my recount of a trip to Thailand to watch my favorite European football team, Tottenham Hotspur of North London, for their preseason tour. The trip in 2023 to Bangkok’s Rajamangala Stadium was spoiled by a monsoon, making the pitch sopping wet and unplayable. In 2022, I traveled to Ibrox Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland to watch Tottenham take on Rangers. It gave me a chance to watch manager Antonio Conte’s new team and see my favorite players, Son and Harry Kane, in person for the first time. As professional sports go, 2022 marked Kane’s final year at the club, finishing his time as Tottenham’s greatest player of all time and its all-time leading goal scorer. Moura was cut loose in May 2023. My focus for my 2023’s preseason trip to Rajamangala Stadium was to say goodbye to the greatest striker the club has ever produced before the English captain was traded to German superpower Bayern Munich. Tottenham hired Ange Postecoglou as their next manager, known for his attacking brand. Nearly two years later, Postecoglou and Son helped lead Tottenham to the Europa League title in May following a season of frustration. Tottenham finished the Premier League season in 17th of 20 teams, just one spot above the relegation zone, after injuries hobbled the lineup from start to finish. Regardless, Spurs made it to the Europa League Final in Bilbao against Manchester United, winning 1-0 to give Tottenham its first trophy in 17 years. But change was immediately on the horizon. Unfortunately, the Post’s vacation schedule the last two years haven’t lined up with Tottenham’s preseason tour. This year, the club played in Hong Kong against Arsenal and in Seoul versus Newcastle. But more importantly, Son announced he was departing from Tottenham Hotspur following their August 3 match against Newcastle, ending his time with the club after 10 years of service. He now plays for LAFC in Major League Soccer, at least giving me more chances to watch him in person in the U.S., albeit for a different team. The changes throughout Tottenham since my last trip to watch them are an unmistakable reminder of the vicious cycle of professional sports. When asked by European football fans or soccer colleagues, ‘Why Tottenham?’ My response has always been, ‘Because they make you work for it.’ Spurs now go into the 2025-26 season without some of its greatest players, Kane and Son, and its first trophy-winning coach in nearly two decades, Postecoglou. Perhaps new manager Thomas Frank can propel Spurs to greater heights. But one thing is for sure; those memories of watching Kane and Son play in Glasgow and walk in the pouring rain in Bangkok are now much more special. 14 Wednesday, August 13, 2025 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 18th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. CHRISTIAN TAYLOR Track and Field Piedmont High Class of 2023 UC Davis Class of 2027 Christian Taylor graduated from Piedmont High in 2023 as a four-year varsity member in both cross country and track and field. He’s set to embark on his junior year at UC Davis. With the Aggies’ track team, Taylor competed in five events last season. He won the 800 at the Aggies Open in March, clocking a time of 1:54.34 in a field of 25 runners. He finished his season in April at the Mike Fanelli Track Classic, placing 37th of 193 in the 800 with a time of 1:54.41, while also finishing 37th of 173 in the 1500, clocking a 3:58.28. He details his workout program ahead of his junior year. What is your workout program this summer? Staff Photo Christian Taylor, PHS Class of 2023, is entering his junior year on the UC Davis track and field team. My workout schedule is the same as it was last year, but with slightly higher mileage. Workouts on Tuesday and Thursday, long runs on Sunday, with Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday being steady runs. I’m going up to 70 miles per week this summer and am currently at 60 miles per week. I am also lifting five days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main fitness goal is to get my Achilles healed with lots of rehab and some treatment. The secondary goal is to just build back my base fitness to prepare for an intensive winter of training. How are you measuring your development? I track all my mileage and workouts to see what my fitness level looks like, but don’t have any direct metrics other than mileage and workout pace. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working on my own, but with training and rehab given to me by my coaches and athletic trainer. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I think the most impressive thing I’ve done this summer was a 14-mile run in Big Bear (6,700 feet) with 1,700 feet of elevation gain throughout the run. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I would tell them that discipline is key. You need to be consistent and work out; especially on the days you don’t feel like it. Those days are what separate the top 1 percent from everyone else. NIA KIM Track and Field Get your FREE estimate today from Piedmont’s most trusted auto body shop. UALITY BODY & FENDER (510) 839-3122 www.QualityBF.com Piedmont High Class of 2025 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2029 Nia Kim was breakout star on Piedmont High’s track and field team in her only year as a varsity athlete after joining the squad as a former gymnast. We named her our 2025 Athlete of the Year award winner. Kim became a Western Alameda County Conference champion on May 7 in the 100 meter hurdles with a time of 15.62 seconds and the North Coast Section Bayshore Area champion in 15.19 on May 17. She logged the same time at the Meet of Champions on May 24 to place sixth overall. This all came after Kim and coach Pouyan Assadi discovered hurdles could become her primary event after randomly jumping over a frame during practice. Nia also placed second of 15 at the WACC Championship in the high jump with a height of five feet. She jumped the same height at the NCS Bayshore Area Championship to place third of 18. She also reached the Meet of Champions on two different relay teams. Her 4x100 team was fifth of 21 at the Bayshore in 50.06 and wound up finishing 17th of 24 at the Meet of Champions in 50.18. Her 4x400 team placed second of 14 at the Bayshore in 4:09.20, while they placed 13th of 23 at the Meet of Champions in 4:09.06. Her time of 15.19 sets the standard at Piedmont High, holding the school record with over a second gap to its next best time, which was Elizabeth Korn’s 16.35 in 2019. She details her workout plan ahead of her freshman year at UC Santa Cruz. What is your workout program this summer? I have been doing lots of strength training, sprint workouts, and mobility work about 4-5 days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I am hoping to improve my explosiveness while also keeping up my endurance for longer distances. I am also trying to prevent injury by doing lots of rehab and weight training. How are you measuring your development? I have been timing my sprints and have been progressively overloading my reps at the gym. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I have been training solo, which can make discipline a little harder, but I occasionally run into my high school coaches. Having company can make my workouts a bit easier and boost my motivation. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I’ve felt myself getting stronger in the weight room and that’s carried into my strength on the field. Staff Photo Nia Kim joins UC Santa Cruz after winning the Post’s 2025 Athlete of the Year award. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I’d recommend taking care of your body by getting enough rest and fuel. Also, trust in the process and in your coaches. It’s helpful to remind yourself that you are your biggest competition, not the people around you. WILL PARKER Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2025 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2029 Will Parker just graduated from Piedmont High, helping them go 16-10 and reach the NCS Quarterfinals. He earned firstteam All-League honors as a junior and senior and was named the Post’s Athlete of the Month in April. Last season, Parker leads the team with a sterling .400 batting average for 32 hits, 19 RBIs, nine doubles, two triples, and one home run. As a junior, Parker was a big factor in the team compiling a 19-10 overall record and winning the WACC Foothill Division regular season with a 7-3 record. PHS battled to the D4 NCS Championship as the No. 2 seed, losing to No. 4 Justin-Siena. They qualified for the D4 CIF State NorCal tournament for the first time. Earning the No. 1 seed, PHS beat No. 8 Capuchino 13-1, won 5-0 over No. 4 Colusa, but lost 6-0 to No. 2 Bradshaw Christian in the championship game. In 2024, Will led the team with a .375 batting average, recording 33 hits with eight doubles, 24 RBIs and scored 22 runs. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I’ve been hitting, lifting, and doing throwing/ defensive work. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals are to continue to put on muscle, get stronger, and build explosiveness to get my body in the right shape to get to work on campus in the fall. How are you measuring your development? I usually base my measurement of development on how much harder I’m throwing and hitting, as well as checking my weight on the scale. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I do my lifting on my own in my home gym, mixing in lifts instructions from the strength coach at Pomona-Pitzer, along with my own lifts. I also go to a coach in San Leandro to work on hitting and defense. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I recently hit 240 pounds on the bench press. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? No one should have to push you to get better. The real work happens when no one’s watching. Silent work makes the loudest impact. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) newest exhibition Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. The exhibition features historical and contemporary posters and photographs to draw comparisons between the strike at SFSU and the recent campus protests against the war in Gaza. In October 2024, San Francisco University State University students protested the Israel-Hamas war and the statewide school system’s ongoing investments in weapons manufacturers. Student-led demonstrations were seen at campuses across the state and at University of California schools. Museum visitors will be presented with an opportunity to integrate local historical context with more recent student demonstrations, including pro-Palestinian organizations on campuses throughout California. Students on Strike is on view through May 31, 2026. Visit https://museumca.org/ on-view/students-on-strike/ to learn more. articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) presents Routed West: Twentieth-Century African American Quilts in California, an exhibition of more than one hundred quilts by approximately eighty artists, on view now through November. African American Quilts is the most expansive presentation to date of a transformative bequest of African American quilts that BAMPFA received in 2019, and highlights the history of the Second Great Migration where African Americans emigrated from the south fleeing economic and racial oppression. Many families settled in California, bringing quiltmaking traditions from the communities they had left behind. Approximately one fourth of the quilts displayed were completed in the South prior to 1950, while others were created in California during the postwar era. articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma to UC Berkeley’s historic Greek Theatre in a special Labor Day weekend performance on Saturday, August 30. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music, and remains one of the world’s most well-respected cellists. The Labor Day concert is part of Cal Performances’ Illuminations: “Exile & Sanctuary” programming for the 2025–26 season, a theme that aims to “conYo-Yo Ma and Angelique Kidjo nect seven unique performances to academic research” on the UC Berkeley campus, focusing on physical displacement, rupture of identity, and “a stripping away of the familiar that leaves an individual or community without a sense of belonging.” The performance connects centuries of interaction between African musical idioms and western music, highlighting exile and sanctuary as both a refuge and a creative space for artists. Ma and Kidjo use the Baroque sarabande dance form and its possible African antecedent, a dance to worship the Congolese spirit Zarabanda as a method to showcase the qualities that connect different cultures, genres, and musical traditions. “Every day there are moments when all of us can feel we are on the inside of something and also when we feel we are on the outside of something,” Ma said in a statement. “To be able to understand both at the same time and oscillate between the two gives us a larger perspective on the world.” “If your mind is open, and there is no fear, it’s easier to listen, and to question yourself,” Kidjo added. Tickets are likely to sell out fast and are currently available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Zellerbach Hall Ticket Office Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m.

articles.text: Consider the still memorable template: The year is 1918. WWI is underway, and for almost two years a pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu, grips the world. Its origin is still unknown, its impact staggering. Some 500 million were infected and 50 to 100 million died. Panic swept the globe; white masks, a signature image, were ubiquitous. Recall Outbreak, released some years back, which opened with an image of an infected person sneezing in a movie theater. It was a hold-your-breath moment as the small particles went aerosol. Contagion has countless such moments, small and large. The film opens with a dark screen and the sound of a dry, hacking cough. Then the image of Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) comes into focus, her face a sheen of sweat. She’s in a nightclub in Macao, gambling, having drinks with business associates, and talking intimately to someone not her husband on a cell phone. She coughs again and is asked if she feels all right. She insists it’s just jet lag. At that moment, the audience knows more than she does: this will not end well. Everything she touches, every person she comes into contact with, warrants a tight shot, and each image is, as is the movie, chilling. The film also flirts, thematically, with apocalypse, touching on how fragile are society’s rules of law and decorum. It soon becomes evident in Contagion that just beneath the patina of civilization resides the instinct for survival at any cost—a Darwinian response that can, like the virus, be just as lethal. The thread of civility is slender. Of course we live as if it were otherwise. However, one event can change everything. Contagion is about such an event. Contagion. Directed by Steven Soderbergh. articles.text: Martin Scorsese has never been afraid to say what he thinks about the art form he’s devoted his life to. But in the age of billion-dollar superhero franchises, his comments about Marvel films landed like a thunderclap—dividing fans, filmmakers, and critics into rival camps. Movies—cinema, film, however we name them—are a technological and artistic wonder, blending writing, acting, photography, costuming, sound, and music into worlds that can thrill, terrify, and move us to tears. They are the modern-day campfire, drawing audiences together to witness stories of danger, triumph, and transformation. And each year, we celebrate the best of them with ceremony, glamour, and awards. It was the question of what best really means that prompted Scorsese to write his controversial New York Times essay, The Dying Art of Filmmaking. In it, he set out to define what cinema is—and isn’t. Just before the release of The Irishman—nominated for 10 Oscars and arguably his magnum opus—Scorsese was asked about Marvel movies. He admitted he’d tried to watch a few but found they weren’t for him. “They are closer to theme parks than they are to movies as I’ve known and loved them… and in the end, I don’t think they’re cinema.” Martin Scorsese – director, producer, screenwriter and actor He praised Marvel’s artistry and technical skill but drew a sharp line between spectacle and substance. “Cinema,” he wrote, “is about revelation—aesthetic, emotional, and spiritual revelation. Thompson), who—along with his sister Marilla (Geraldine James)—had requested a teenage boy from an orphanage to help on their farm, instead finds Anne, a spirited redhead with boundless curiosity and a torrent of words. A mistake has been made, but Matthew reluctantly brings her home, unaware that Anne has not yet truly found a family. Anne is precocious, imaginative, and resilient—traits that both charm and unsettle those around her. Her rich inner world is a refuge from the cruelty and loss she has endured since birth. Across three seasons, the series offers superb performances and tackles themes that remain timely today, extending well beyond the typical scope of an adolescent coming-of-age tale. While particularly resonant for tween and teen girls, it’s a series worth watching together as a family, sparking meaningful conversations. Unless revived by popular demand, there will be no fourth season—but Anne With An E is still not to be missed. Anne With An E. Directed by Moira Walley-Beckett. Starring Amybeth McNulty, R.H. Thompson, Geraldine James. Three seasons. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Netflix. articles.text: Have you ever returned home to what looks like an explosion of cushion stuffing and trash, courtesy of your furry friend? Destroying items, inappropriate elimination, excessive vocalizing, and obsessive scratching are all symptoms of a common issue known as separation anxiety. Many modern pet parents treat their dogs like family members, taking them everywhere, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic. However, failing to establish the need for occasional alone time can be a disservice to your dog. Dogs are pack animals that respond to their world partially based on the reactions of the one in charge of their safety. Establishing a clear hierarchy helps them understand what’s expected of them and can increase their feeling of safety in your home and with you. A dog that feels responsible for you will spend a great deal of time worrying about making decisions regarding safety, whereas a dog that feels responsible to you knows you can keep them safe. So, how do you address separation anxiety in your dog? Let’s go back to puppy 101; where do we put a puppy to bed before they’ve been house trained? Most would answer correctly: the crate. Crate training can be an effective way to address separation anxiety. The goal is to establish a safe space to which your dog knows you will always return. To start, acquire a crate and leave the door open. Stand a few feet away, toss treats into the crate, and tell your dog to “go to bed.” Let them begin to associate their crate with the yummy things you’re tossing in there. Once your dog is comfortable entering the crate, tell them to lay down, then to stay. Walk away to the other side of the room, and come back to give them a treat. Repeat this process with longer and longer distances. Now it’s time to close the door when you walk away, but make sure to open it 90% of the time when you come back. If your dog cries in the crate or paws at the door, use a firm sharp voice to discourage this behavior. Make sure you never return to the crate unless your dog is quiet to avoid accidentally rewarding poor behavior with your presence. Start with short periods of crate time with you out of sight (like thirty seconds), and gradually increase that time. Never crate a dog for longer than four hours. To make the crate a happy space, leave the door open when not using it and slip delicious tidbits into the crate so your dog feels interested in returning to check for rewards. With patience and consistency, crate training can help your dog feel more secure and reduce separation anxiety. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped to found the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. The group was pleased to have Heidi Schmidt and Mary Carter with them for the first time. The group was there to talk about their August book, Tender At The Bone: Growing Up At The Table by Ruth Reichl. She is an American chef, food writer, New York Times restaurant critic, and has also written cookbooks, memoirs, and a novel. This debut 1998 memoir is full of life and love, loss and survival, and is especially about food. It was on The New York Times bestseller list several weeks. There are the food stories and recipes that shaped her life, but Reichl also shares stories of her family, friendships, and her journey of self-discovery. She learned early in life that since she wasn’t “pretty or funny or sexy,” but she could attract friends with food instead. Throughout the book there are humorous stories and her favorite recipes. Reichl was raised in Manhattan and Connecticut by a docile father and a mother who suffered from manic depression. She enjoyed the advantages of some family wealth, such as a Christmas in Paris when she was 13, and high school in Canada to learn French. She went to the University of Michigan, earned a graduate degree in art history, married a sculptor, lived in a loft in Manhattan, and then in the 1970s with friends bought a 17-room “cottage” in Berkeley that they turned into a commune and restaurant. The reading group alternates between fiction and non-books. August was a non-fiction month, but at the discussion’s start the possibility was raised that Tender At The Bone is actually fiction. Many of Reichl’s adventures seemed to be exaggerated and embellished. Could her mother really be a notorious food poisoner and known as the “Queen of Mold?” In fact, Reichl confessed the book was mostly true and some was made up for entertaining storytelling. Some readers found the book to be fun and it didn’t matter if all the stories were completely true, but others didn’t want to finish the book. For food-oriented readers the inclusion of recipes was enjoyable and the ones for Reichl’s devil eggs and brownies were considered the best. Members of the group could also relate to Reichl’s experiences in the New York City area, Michigan, and Berkeley, which all seemed accurate and were engaging. There were times when readers laughed out loud at the usual behavior of the Reichl family. The author’s relationships with her parents were particularly interesting. Her mother was mentally ill and her behavior and choices for Reichl when she was young created strange situations. But her father didn’t intervene. He used his work to escape the craziness and Reichl used food to escape too. Readers thought the family was in denial about the mother being bipolar. The fact that both of the father’s two wives were mentally ill said something about him too. However, it was noted that people didn’t fully understand mental illness and didn’t talk about it at that time. Another interesting side discussion was how non-Jews interpret actions by Jews that are considered part of their Jewish identity (e.g., eating pork). It was also fun to note that “old fashion” items like a rotary phone or phonograph record are unknown objects to grandchildren. Readers’ criticisms of the book were many. It didn’t capture their interest. It was repetitive and like a soap opera; it wasn’t exciting. The story was always about her, but not self-revelatory; other characters weren’t well developed. However, it was accepted that this is a memoir and this focus on the author might be expected. There was a desire to know more about Reichl’s later professional life, but that was probably another book too. It was also noted that the book’s title, Tender At The Bone, actually refers to being vulnerable. Reichl was able to overcome the challenges created by her parents though her drive and intellect and also with the support of other family members, the family cook, and business mentors. She came out of her family chaos fine and successful. This was something the readers could all appreciate. The group had previously selected The Women by Kristin Hannah for September and The Wright Brothers by David McCullough for October. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh’s presentation of three fiction candidates the readers chose Euphoria by Lily King for their November book. Since Labor Day is Monday, September 1, the group will meet on Sept ember 8 at 1:30 p.m. for their next discussion. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. There was an excellent turnout of 24 readers on August 4th for the First Mondays Reading Group discussion.

Understanding separation anxiety in dogs By Sierra Berrick Have you ever returned home to what looks like an explosion of cushion stuffing and trash, courtesy of your furry friend? Destroying items, inappropriate elimination, excessive vocalizing, and obsessive scratching are all symptoms of a common issue known as separation anxiety. Many modern pet parents treat their dogs like family members, taking them everywhere, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic. However, failing to establish the need for occasional alone time can be a disservice to your dog. Dogs are pack animals that respond to their world partially based on the reactions of the one in charge of their safety. Establishing a clear hierarchy helps them understand what’s expected of them and can increase their feeling of safety in your home and with you. A dog that feels responsible for you will spend a great deal of time worrying about making decisions regarding safety, whereas a dog that feels responsible to you knows you can keep them safe. So, how do you address separation anxiety in your dog? Let’s go back to puppy 101; where do we put a puppy to bed before they’ve been house trained? Most would answer correctly: the crate. Crate training can be an effective way to address separation anxiety. The goal is to establish a safe space to which your dog knows you will always return. To start, acquire a crate and leave the door open. Stand a few feet away, toss treats into the crate, and tell your dog to “go to bed.” Let them begin to associate their crate with the yummy things you’re tossing in there. Once your dog is comfortable entering the crate, tell them to lay down, then to stay. Walk away to the other side of the room, and come back to give them a treat. Repeat this process with longer and longer distances. Now it’s time to close the door when you walk away, but make sure to open it 90% of the time when you come back. If your dog cries in the crate or paws at the door, use a firm sharp voice to discourage this behavior. Make sure you never return to the crate unless your dog is quiet to avoid accidentally rewarding poor behavior with your presence. Start with short periods of crate time with you out of sight (like thirty seconds), and gradually increase that time. Never crate a dog for longer than four hours. To make the crate a happy space, leave the door open when not using it and slip delicious tidbits into the crate so your dog feels interested in returning to check for rewards. With patience and consistency, crate training can help your dog feel more secure and reduce separation anxiety. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped to found the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: The Rockridge district will be rockin’ on Saturday, August 23 with more than 20 street performances, 55 local artists, flea and artisan market, big sales and special offers, kids’ crafts, special menus and tastings, and a pup promenade. Rockridge welcomes everyone to the Rockridge Rock-NStroll enjoy local wares, fine dining, savory sweets, and delicious drinks found only in this magical district. This is not a typical street festival. It’s a 1-mile leisurely stroll loaded with amazing sights, sounds, and experiences on every block. From Broadway to Alcatraz, College Avenue and its side streets will be full of creativity and family-friendly finds. Rock-N-Stroll is a true showcase of one of Oakland’s most creative and vibrant neighborhoods. A vast majority of the musicians and artists participating in the event hail from Rockridge itself, either living or working in the district. These talented artists of all ages will be performing or tabling inside and outside of shops, each matched with a location that best compliments their style. On this one day, the entire district turns into a carefully-curated local arts gallery. “As a proud Oakland resident involved in the art scene here, I am always in awe of the incredible local artists that live in our neighborhoods,” said Marcy Reed, a festival volunteer that who spearheads the outreach for artists. Over 20 street performers will be spread out on nearly every other block of the district to entertain you during your stroll. Representing a range of musical styles from a solo cellist to a 5-piece Tom Petty tribute band, they provide the perfect ambiance for a day of exploring Rockridge. Because there are no stages or street closures, you will want to bring your own lawn chair if you want to park yourself near a band. Stores, restaurants, salons, and other service providers will be offering special promotions for visitors. You can sample free tacos at Belly, grab a free book from the Rockridge Library, paint piggy banks at First Federal Savings & Loan, spin a prize wheel at Market Hall, get 50% off an item from Cole Hardware, along with other offers from over 40 businesses. For more details and a schedule of activities, visit RockridgeDistrict.com/rocknstroll. articles.text: Earlier this summer, longtime Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick released Ripley’s Bird Buddies, the fourth installment of a self-published, illustrated children’s series based on the adventures of their late rescue cat Ripley. The newly-published story became the Herricks’ “own little bird book,” Connie Herrick said, identifying 20 different species of birds that live in Piedmont. It was a natural progression for Ripley’s story, she added, which began in 2021 with Ripley’s World, the Herricks’ first book of the series. Each book features titular character Ripley, a “tiny, feisty, funny, calico kitty with a big imagination,” and is bolstered by her many real-life friends in Piedmont including her German Shepherd “sisters” Kapo and Pele, raccoon twins, baby possums, and a squirrel that plays tag. Ripley’s Bird Buddies celebrates the city’s diverse avian wildlife and was coincidentally released as Piedmont became a hotspot among avid birdwatchers and environmentalists. A pair of great horned owls took up residence in Dracena Park earlier this year, and more recently, a family of bald eagles in a eucalyptus tree on the Piedmont-Oakland border has garnered a sizable, local following for marking the first time in recorded history that the species has successfully raised babies in the city, according to NBC Bay Area. This renewed interest highlights the core message of Ripley’s Bird Buddies, which encourages young readers to “take a moment every day to enjoy and know the birds in your neighborhood.” It includes a lengthy list of bird species that are easily identifiable in Piedmont, the natural setting of all Ripley’s books, including the white-crowned sparrow, California scrub jay, and mourning dove The inspiration for Ripley’s Bird Buddies came organically, Connie explained, from observing birds that have gathered in the couple’s own backyard over the years. Mark Herrick, who illustrates the children’s books, was separately working on paintings of finches and jays that became regulars at their Greenbank house. “I told Mark, these bird paintings that you’re doing are really nice. I think we ought to do a book,” Connie said. “I thought kids would really like to know about [the birds’] little personalConnie and Mark Herrick Mark Herrick at work illustrating Ripley’s Missing Locket, the couple’s second book, in watercolor. Cover of Ripley’s Bird Buddies ities, because they’re very, very distinctive. The way they interact with each other, and their special little quirks, really identify them.” Mark’s illustrations and Connie’s writing describe each species in kid-friendly detail, including their distinctive coloring, favorite garden snacks, and birdsong cadence. “As we were going through these [illustrations] and creating personalities for the birds, we started to block out and storyboard.” Mark said. “It was very organic and unplanned, and we had a lot of fun with it.” Connie said she started “gathering facts” about crows, juncos, hummingbirds and falcons for the story. “I started writing these little vignettes for each bird based on the facts but it was really boring. It was boring to me, and it was certainly going to be boring to the child, so I shifted my focus on their personalities and how they interact with each other,” she said. “For example, the house finch is a bit of a bully,” she said with a laugh. “But the little lesser Goldfinch, the ones that are yellow, those poor things, they just get knocked off.” New characters include Kangee, the American Crow, a “brave, bold, tricky trickster who loves to pull funny pranks,” and Kali, a Dark-eyed Junco, who is a “really good scratcher and digger and can find hidden treats like juicy, wild berries.” They are joined by a pair of “large and powerful” owls, an “aerobatic” Peregrine Falcon, a pair of “shy but friendly” mourning doves and more. The Herricks said they hope Ripley’s Bird Buddies will inspire a new generation of birdwatchers, and admit that they weren’t invested in the hobby until receiving a gift from friend and former Piedmont mayor Patty White, who passed away in 2023. Patty gave the Herricks a birdfeeder when they were mourning the passing of their dog. “That was really the beginning of it all,” Mark said. “We just got so super into it because we just lost Kapo, and were grieving and trying to figure out, do we get another dog or not? Then we set up the feeder, and the birds and squirrels really became like our outdoor pets,” he said. “We just got so much pleasure, sitting there drinking our coffee and getting to know the personalities of these birds. It was a huge, huge positive force in our life.” Copies of Ripley’s Bird Buddies and other books in the series are available online at www. RipleyandFriendz.com. The Herrick’s fifth book, Ripley’s Vet Visit, will be published in 2026.

Walkers explore history of Frank Havens By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was a warm day so the Walking on Wednesdays group decided to stay in the central part of Piedmont and the shade of Wildwood Gardens for their weekly walk. Wildwood Gardens was the site of Frank C. Havens’ early 20th Century “Wildwood Estate” so there was lots of Piedmont history to be discussed. There was a historical connection with Frank C. Havens at 801 Magnolia, which is now the home of the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA). The first building at 801 Magnolia was built as a private residence around 1878. It is reported to have been a twin of the Wetmore House up Bonita Avenue at its corner with Vista Avenue and is considered to be Piedmont’s oldest unaltered home. It was built in 1878 for Jesse Wetmore and his family as a summer home. Frank C. Havens was born in 1848 into one of the founding families of Shelter Island, New York. He ran away from home at the age of sixteen and became a cabin boy on a sailing vessel which rounded the Horn on its way to California. He spent two years in Honolulu and went to China. After a year in the China shipping trade, he Wednesday Walkers meet new Piedmont Police Chief, Frederick Shavies. came to San Francisco in 1866. He worked in banking and became an Oakland attorney and real estate developer in the East Bay, particularly in Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont. Havens was married twice. His first wife died when she was 33 and his second wife was Lila Mandana Rand. The Havens family lived in the house at 801 Magnolia, which was the home of Blanche Wetmore Sherman. This location was convenient for Havens, as it was across from Piedmont Park which he was developing. Records show that the house was remodeled and converted into a Christian Science Church in 1935. A youth education wing was added in 1964. The Christian Science Church building was purchased by the City of Piedmont in 2003 as part of its Civic Center Master Plan, which later stalled. After sitting vacant for years, the City leased the building to the PCA which began renovations in 2011 for its use as an arts center. In about 1880 Havens founded a stock brokerage and then created the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” in 1895 with F.M. “Borax” Smith. Through it Havens and Smith built the Claremont Hotel and other structures. The Syndicate was also originally the parent company of the Key System transit company and accumulated at least 13,000 aces of valuable hilltop land that stretched from near Mills College to the boundary of North Berkeley. The group walked up Highland Avenue and down Wildwood Avenue to the entrance of Wildwood Gardens. Two partially hidden columns mark the former entrance to Havens’ estate. The walkers entered the neighborhood and made their way through its streets. They noted a unique brick storybook home with a curved roof while looking for 101 Wildwood Gardens, Havens’ mansion. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue down to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road and wanted to build his estate on this land. In 1906 Havens hired Bernard Maybeck to design his home. It was designed as an oriental home of teakwood and fine carvings from India, China and Japan. It took two years to build. Havens was also a follower of Eastern philosophy and meditation, and the mansion had an opium smoking bed.
